headline: Chinook Salmon Thrive After Klamath River Dams Come Down
meta_description: Two years after four dams were removed, 20,000 chinook salmon have migrated up the Klamath River—a faster recovery than scientists anticipated.
summary_short: Two years after dam removal, 20,000 chinook salmon have returned to the Klamath River in Oregon and California. Scientists say the biological response exceeded expectati…
body:
Two years after the removal of four dams from the Klamath River, which flows through southern Oregon and northern California, chinook salmon have staged a remarkable comeback. A new study documents that 20,000 of these fish have migrated upstream, demonstrating that the decades-old restoration effort is working faster than anticipated. Damon Goodman, the lead author of the study, expressed surprise at the speed of recovery: "The biological response has been much faster than I, and most of us, expected."

The return of fall-run salmon represents a tangible win for river restoration advocates who have long argued that removing dams would revitalize ecosystems and fish populations. The Klamath's recovery is particularly significant because it shows that large-scale environmental restoration can yield measurable results within a relatively short timeframe. Yet the work remains incomplete. Two dams still stand along the river, and ongoing debates about water allocation continue to shape the river's future.

While challenges persist, the presence of 20,000 chinook swimming upstream is undeniable evidence of progress—a sign that nature can rebound when given the chance. For communities and conservationists invested in the Klamath's health, this biological milestone offers something increasingly rare: hope grounded in hard data.
quick_facts: 20,000 chinook salmon migrated up the Klamath River in two years
Four dams were removed from the Klamath River in southern Oregon and northern California
Study lead Damon Goodman: recovery faster than expected
Two dams remain on the river
